messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 27-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a rideshare driver in a mid-sized American city. He came to the intake session quietly, choosing the seat farthest from the door, and spoke in measured sentences that occasionally broke apart when the material became too close. He has never sought mental health support before. What finally brought him in, he said, was that he had nearly driven his car off an overpass three weeks ago — not by accident.

The abuse began when Kwame was around six and continued until he was fourteen, carried out by his father, a man who worked nights and came home in the early hours smelling of alcohol and something else Kwame still cannot name. The worst episodes followed a particular pattern: Kwame would hear the slow, heavy footsteps on the wooden hallway floor outside his bedroom, and the sound alone was enough to make his body lock. His father favoured the cold — winter mornings, the window left open — and Kwame learned to associate the bite of cold air on his skin with what was about to happen. The beatings often involved a leather belt, and the specific texture of that material — rough, cracked, slightly warm from his father's hand — became encoded into those nights in a way that no amount of time has fully erased.

Kwame left his family home at seventeen and has not returned. He moved through community college, a series of jobs, and eventually into rideshare driving, which suited him because he could control the environment, control who entered and left, and, crucially, drive away. But the cab of his car has not been the sanctuary he imagined. Passengers sometimes wear belts with a particular texture he catches in his peripheral mirror. In winter, cold air floods the car when someone opens the door, and the temperature on his skin — that specific chill — arrives before any conscious thought does, and his body is already somewhere else. When a passenger walks up behind the car or he hears footsteps approaching on a quiet street, his nervous system responds as if the hallway outside his childhood bedroom still exists. These triggers hit him without warning, and in the moments after, he finds himself either driving recklessly — taking corners too fast, running yellow lights, doing things he recognises are dangerous — or reaching for the small bag of marijuana he keeps in the centre console, smoking between fares to bring his heart rate down. He has also begun using harder substances on weekends. The distraction and the drugs work, in the short term, which is why he keeps returning to them.

What Kwame has come to believe about himself is perhaps more disabling than any single symptom. He is certain that he has been permanently changed — that something essential was broken in those years that cannot be repaired. The phrase he used in session was: "I'm not the same as other people my age." He has pulled away from the Ghanaian community his mother once kept him connected to, skipping the church gatherings and cultural events he attended through his twenties, convinced that the disconnection he feels is visible, that people can see what was done to him. This belief that he is fundamentally altered deepens the sense that he cannot be safe anywhere — that even when a situation is objectively calm, his body's insistence on reacting as though danger is present proves that he cannot trust reassurance from others or from his own circumstances. This appraisal of himself as permanently damaged has pushed him further into isolation, keeping intimacy at a distance and reinforcing the drug use as the only reliable management tool he has — which, over months, has stripped away more of the community and connection that might otherwise have contradicted his darkest beliefs about himself.

The hypervigilance and the avoidance now feed each other in ways Kwame is beginning to dimly recognise. The more he monitors for threat — scanning every fare, tracking footsteps on the street outside his car — the more his body stays primed, and the more primed his body stays, the more easily the triggers find him. He came to the intake session, he said, not because he believes he can be fixed, but because he is tired of being afraid of himself. What he hopes for, tentatively, is to understand why his body keeps doing this to him. What he fears most is that the answer will confirm what he already suspects: that it always will.
